title: Jump Game III
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<bool> visited: n entries → O(n)
- queue<int> q: up to n entries → O(n)
- recursion depth: none (iterative)
- not counted: input arr
approach: Treat each index as a node in an implicit graph with at most two outgoing edges: `i + arr[i]` and `i - arr[i]`. Starting from `start`, perform BFS: enqueue the start, mark visited, and for each dequeued index check if `arr[i] == 0` (return true), otherwise enqueue both in-bounds, unvisited neighbors. If the queue empties without finding a zero, return false. Each index is visited at most once, guaranteeing termination even with cycles.
hints: From any index i, you can land on exactly two positions: i + arr[i] and i - arr[i]. Starting from `start` and following those jumps, could you ever arrive at the same index more than once? If so, what must you remember to avoid exploring forever?
Use BFS with a queue and a boolean visited array. In Example 1, start at index 5 (arr[5] = 1): enqueue 5+1 = 6 and 5−1 = 4, mark both visited, then dequeue 6 next.

```
visited = [false] * n
queue = [start]
visited[start] = true
while queue not empty:
    i = dequeue
    if arr[i] == 0: return true
    for next in [i + arr[i], i - arr[i]]:
        if 0 <= next < n and not visited[next]:
            visited[next] = true
            enqueue next
return false
```

**Single element** - the array has exactly one element.
`Input: arr = [0], start = 0` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: adding `if (n == 1) return false` as a premature base case → returns false

**No zeros** - no index contains 0, so no valid landing exists.
`Input: arr = [1,1,1,1], start = 0` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: returning true when the queue empties → returns true

**Cycle without zero** - all jumps lead back to already-visited indices.
`Input: arr = [2,2,2,2,2], start = 0` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: marking visited at dequeue instead of enqueue → infinite loop, TLE

**Start is zero** - the starting index already holds value 0.
`Input: arr = [3,0,2,1,2], start = 1` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: checking `arr[neighbor] == 0` instead of `arr[i] == 0` at dequeue; arr[1]=0 produces no unvisited neighbors → returns false

followUps.q: Find the minimum number of jumps to reach any index with value 0.
followUps.a: BFS already explores in order of increasing distance, so track a level counter (or store distance alongside each index in the queue). Return the distance when arr[i] == 0 is first found. TC: O(n), SC: O(n).

followUps.q: What if you can also jump to any index j where arr[j] == arr[i] (Jump Game IV style)?
followUps.a: Build a map from value to list of indices once, then BFS using three neighbor types: i+arr[i], i−arr[i], and all indices sharing arr[i]. Clear the map entry for a value after first use to avoid re-processing. TC: O(n), SC: O(n).

followUps.q: Solve with O(1) auxiliary space (modifying the input is allowed).
followUps.a: Mark visited indices in-place by negating arr[i] (all values are non-negative). Use an explicit stack/queue stored inside the array itself is not feasible, so use iterative DFS with the call simulated via the array - alternatively, since arr[i] < n, set arr[i] = n as a sentinel and recurse. TC: O(n), SC: O(1) auxiliary (input modified).
